newsitem.title: USA: Subdued US data throw wrench in Fed hike prospects.
newsitem.headline: Subdued US data throw wrench in Fed hike prospects.

text.p: Just when a Federal Reserve interest rate hike appeared to be a near certainty, a series of subdued reports on inflation and retail sales has severely clouded the prospects for tighter U.S. monetary policy, economists said on Friday.

Although many Fed watchers are sticking to their guns and predicting a 25-basis-point hike to short-term rates at the September 24 Federal Open Market Committee meeting, they admit this week's data provide ample ammunition to the doves within the central bank who would prefer to leave policy unchanged.

Without any concrete signs that inflation is on the rise and given the sensitive nature of monetary policy during a presidential election year, policymakers who feel the need to step on the brakes now have a harder sell later this month.

"Today's reports certainly give the doves some more ammunition," said Sung Won Sohn, chief economist at Minneapolis-based Norwest Corp. "They will try to argue that the economy is already slowing down and the hawks will say it isn't slowing down fast enough. It is clearly a very complicated situation."

After reporting a reassuring drop in August core producer prices on Thursday, the Labor Department announced Friday that consumer prices had risen a paltry 0.1 percent in both the overall and core readings in the month.

The Commerce Department's release of surprisingly tepid August retail sales data on Friday -- showing a meager 0.2-percent rise in both overall and ex-autos readings -- cast further doubt on rate hike prospects, economists said.
Both Treasury and stock market prices, reflecting revised thinking on Fed policy, posted sharp gains on the data.

"The recent data do not alter the picture in my mind, but I'm sure it will change the picture in many others," said Richard Berner, chief economist and executive vice president at Pittsburgh-based Mellon Bank. "That is clearly reflected in the marketplace."

Berner said the tepid retail sales numbers confirm that consumers "took a breather" during the summer. He cautioned however, that strong job and income growth suggest an imminent consumer comeback and said forward-looking Fed policy should take the likelihood of such a rebound into account.

Berner's comments touched on the central dilemma for Fed policymakers -- whether to react to clear warning signals that inflation may take off in the near future, or to wait for concrete evidence that inflation pressures are manifesting themselves.

Recent comments from Fed officials -- including so-called monetary doves -- have suggested that labor market tightness and above-trend growth could be enough to prompt a rate hike, even in the absence of consumer price pressures.
But in the wake of Friday's numbers, many market participants clearly feel the tide may have turned.
"Probabilities have shifted back in the direction of no action...and the market is clearly unwinding expectations of tightening," said Paul McCulley, chief economist at UBS Securities.
McCulley is betting the Fed will stand pat at the upcoming FOMC meeting. He said Friday's economic data only reinforce his conviction that policymakers can take a wait-and-see approach.
"Regardless of which camp you're in, you now have evidence to sit on your hands," he said.
